# Clinical Data Standards: CDISC, SDTM, and ADaM {#sec-cdisc} Alumni of this program who now work for pharmaceutical sponsors and contract research organizations (CROs) report the same first week: data structures, variable names, and regulatory conventions that their statistics courses never mentioned. One of those conventions produces a wrong answer without an error. The time-to-event datasets they are handed code an event as `CNSR = 0` and censoring as a positive number, the reverse of what `survival::Surv()` expects, so `Surv(AVAL, CNSR)` runs, draws a plausible curve, and estimates the curve of censoring instead of the curve of events. This chapter builds the standard datasets for the running HF-HOME trial, from the tabulation layer a sponsor submits to the analysis datasets you will specify and check, and shows where each convention can go silently wrong. ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *The nice thing about standards is that you have so many to choose from.* [Andrew S. Tanenbaum]{.smallcaps}, *Computer Networks* (attributed; wording and page vary by edition) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where this chapter sits: deriving analysis datasets from the submitted tabulations is part of the Wrangle stage, which turns raw tables into the derived analytic datasets.](19-cdisc_files/figure-html/fig-cdisc-pipeline-diagram-1.png){#fig-cdisc-pipeline-diagram fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Wrangle.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'} **Reading time.** About 30 minutes. **You'll need.** @sec-joins for declared join relationships, @sec-analysis-plan-estimands for the HF-HOME estimand, and @sec-types for dates. The code uses: ```r library(dplyr) library(survival) library(survminer) library(gtsummary) ``` It also sources the HF-HOME generator, `R/hfhome.R`, which needs no packages beyond base R. **You'll be able to.** - Trace a trial's data from the case report form through SDTM and ADaM to the tables of a clinical study report, and name who builds each layer. - Derive a subject-level dataset (`ADSL`) and a time-to-event dataset (`ADTTE`) from SDTM domains, with randomization dates and population flags drawn from the right source. - Convert the CDISC censoring code correctly at the boundary with `survival::Surv()`, and verify the event count against an independent derivation. - Name the R tools a sponsor uses for tables, package validation, and double programming, and what each checks. **Outline.** - [From protocol to submission](#sec-cdisc-pipeline) - [SDTM: the data as collected](#sec-cdisc-sdtm) - [ADaM: the data as analyzed](#sec-cdisc-adam) - [Worked example: ADSL and ADTTE for HF-HOME](#sec-cdisc-worked) - [Industry practice: tables, validation, double programming](#sec-cdisc-industry) ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Skip ahead?'} If these answers come quickly, skip to the next chapter. The answers are in @sec-quiz-answers-19. 1. What is the difference between SDTM and ADaM, and who typically specifies and builds ADaM? 2. In the CDISC convention, does `CNSR = 1` indicate a censored observation or an event? 3. What is the role of `ADSL` relative to other ADaM datasets such as `ADLB` or `ADTTE`? ::: ## From protocol to submission {#sec-cdisc-pipeline} The Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium (CDISC) is a non-profit that publishes data standards for clinical research. Since December 2016, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has required study data in CDISC formats for new drug applications (NDAs) and biologics license applications (BLAs) [@fda2024conformance]. Of the CDISC standards, two are the statistician's daily material: the Study Data Tabulation Model (SDTM), the submitted record of what was collected, and the Analysis Data Model (ADaM), the datasets the analyses run on.[^cdash] [^cdash]: Two other CDISC standards sit on either side of these. CDASH (Clinical Data Acquisition Standards Harmonization) standardizes the case report form, so that collected fields map cleanly to SDTM; SEND (Standard for Exchange of Nonclinical Data) is SDTM's counterpart for animal studies. ### The pipeline and who builds each layer @fig-cdisc-pipeline shows the flow and the row granularity at each stage, which is the quantity to track across every join. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-cdisc-pipeline %%| fig-alt: "Vertical pipeline from protocol and SAP, to the CRF %%| for site data entry, to SDTM domains such as DM, EX, AE, LB, %%| VS and DS holding one row per observation, to analysis-ready %%| ADaM datasets such as ADSL, ADTTE and ADAE, to tables, %%| listings and figures, and finally to the CSR and FDA %%| submission. Dashed annotations mark SDTM as immutable once %%| locked and ADaM as traceable back to SDTM." %%| fig-cap: "The regulatory data pipeline from protocol to FDA %%| submission. SDTM is the immutable source the analysis reads; %%| ADaM is the analysis-ready layer derived from it." flowchart TD P["Protocol and SAP
design, endpoints, estimands"] --> C["CRF
site data entry"] C --> S["SDTM domains
DM · EX · AE · LB · VS · DS
one row per observation"] S --> A["ADaM datasets
ADSL · ADTTE · ADAE
analysis-ready"] A --> T["TLFs
tables, listings, figures"] T --> R["CSR and FDA submission
Define-XML, aCRF, SDRG, ADRG"] S -.->|"immutable once locked"| S A -.->|"traceable to SDTM"| S ``` The protocol and statistical analysis plan (SAP) define the trial; sites record observations on case report forms (CRFs); data management builds the SDTM domains from the collected data; ADaM datasets are derived from SDTM; and the tables, listings, and figures (TLFs) of the clinical study report (CSR) are produced from ADaM. In most sponsors and CROs the work on ADaM is divided. The biostatistician writes the SAP and, often, the ADaM specifications; statistical programmers implement the datasets and the TLFs against those specifications, usually with independent double programming as validation (@sec-cdisc-industry). Whichever role you take, your deliverables will be ADaM specifications, ADaM datasets, or the tables built from them. Two rules organize the pipeline. **Immutability**: once SDTM is locked it is not edited to suit a new analysis; a new analytic need produces a new ADaM variable. **Traceability**: every ADaM variable points back to its SDTM source and its derivation, recorded in the ADaM specification and in Define-XML. The order of work follows from the second rule: write the specification, review it, then implement it. Building the dataset first and writing the specification from the result is a common antipattern, because the specification is the contract that gets reviewed. ### The submission package A submission carries more than datasets. @tbl-cdisc-package lists the supporting documents a statistician meets; you will rarely write Define-XML by hand, because tools generate it from the specification. | Document | What it is | Typically produced by | |---|---|---| | Define-XML | Machine-readable metadata for every variable: type, controlled terminology, derivation, source | Generated from the specifications | | Annotated CRF (aCRF) | The blank CRF with SDTM variable names on each field | Data management | | Study Data Reviewer's Guide (SDRG) | Narrative on SDTM conformance and known issues | Data management | | Analysis Data Reviewer's Guide (ADRG) | Narrative on ADaM datasets and analysis choices | Statistics and programming | | SAP | Pre-specified analyses, analysis sets, estimands, sensitivity analyses | Biostatistician | : The documents that accompany SDTM and ADaM in a submission. {#tbl-cdisc-package} ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** SDTM already holds every collected value in a one-row-per-observation layout, and ADaM adds no new data. Why build a second layer rather than fit the model on SDTM? **Answer.** Because ADaM is where the analysis decisions become explicit, traceable, and reviewable one at a time: which subjects are in each analysis set, which date starts the clock, how censoring was assigned, which visit is baseline. Fit the model on SDTM and those decisions are still made, but inside the modeling script, mixed together, visible only to whoever reads the code. The separation is the book's raw and derived data rule (@sec-acquisition): SDTM is `data/raw/`, ADaM is `data/derived/`. ::: ## SDTM: the data as collected {#sec-cdisc-sdtm} SDTM organizes a trial's observations into [**domains**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-domain), each a dataset on one topic. The ones you will meet first are `DM` (demographics, one row per subject), `EX` (exposure, one row per dose or dosing interval), `DS` (disposition, one row per milestone or event), `AE` (adverse events), `LB` (laboratory results), and `VS` (vital signs). Within a domain each row is a single observation, and the same variable names (`USUBJID`, `VISIT`, `--TESTCD`, `--ORRES`, `--STRESN`) recur across domains. Dates are ISO 8601 character strings such as `'2024-03-15'` or `'2024-03-15T08:30'`, not `Date` values, because a collected date can be partial (`'2024-03'`) and a character field holds it as collected. ### The HF-HOME domains The HF-HOME generator includes `hfhome_sdtm()`, which builds minimal `DM`, `EX`, and `DS` domains from the trial: `EX` has one row per home-health visit, the intervention in this trial, and `DS` has a `RANDOMIZED` protocol milestone for every subject and one disposition event (`COMPLETED` at day 30, `DEATH`, or `LOST TO FOLLOW-UP` for an unascertained outcome). Readmissions belong in the healthcare-encounters domain, `HO`, which the chunk builds from the outcome file. Real SDTM has many more variables per domain; these keep only what the ADaM derivations need. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(survival) source(file.path('..', '..', 'R', 'hfhome.R')) sdtm <- hfhome_sdtm() dm <- sdtm$dm ex <- sdtm$ex ds <- sdtm$ds hf_dir <- file.path('..', 'data', 'raw_data', 'hfhome') read_hf <- function(file) { readr::read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, file), col_types = readr::cols(patient_id = 'c', .default = '?')) } ho <- read_hf('outcomes.csv') |> filter(!is.na(readmit_date)) |> transmute(STUDYID = 'HFHOME', DOMAIN = 'HO', USUBJID = paste('HFHOME', patient_id, sep = '-'), HOTERM = 'HOSPITAL READMISSION', HOSTDTC = format(readmit_date, '%Y-%m-%d')) c(DM = nrow(dm), EX = nrow(ex), DS = nrow(ds), HO = nrow(ho)) #> DM EX DS HO #> 2432 2237 4864 429 head(select(dm, USUBJID, SITEID, RFSTDTC, AGE, SEX, ARM, ACTARM), 3) #> USUBJID SITEID RFSTDTC AGE SEX ARM ACTARM #> 1 HFHOME-0001 02 2024-02-01 77 F Home health Home health #> 2 HFHOME-0002 05 2024-02-01 77 F Home health Home health #> 3 HFHOME-0003 05 2024-02-01 62 F Usual care Home health head(select(ds, USUBJID, DSDECOD, DSCAT, DSSTDTC), 4) #> USUBJID DSDECOD DSCAT DSSTDTC #> 1 HFHOME-0001 RANDOMIZED PROTOCOL MILESTONE 2024-02-01 #> 2 HFHOME-0001 COMPLETED DISPOSITION EVENT 2024-03-02 #> 3 HFHOME-0002 RANDOMIZED PROTOCOL MILESTONE 2024-02-01 #> 4 HFHOME-0002 COMPLETED DISPOSITION EVENT 2024-03-02 ``` ::: `ARM` is the planned arm, as randomized. `ACTARM` is the arm the subject actually received, here home health if a visit occurred within 7 days of discharge; the two differ for the nonadherent patients in both arms. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Confirm the structural promises of each domain before deriving anything from it: one `DM` row per subject, character dates, two `DS` rows per subject, and no `EX` or `HO` subject missing from `DM`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot( !anyDuplicated(dm$USUBJID), is.character(dm$RFSTDTC), is.character(ex$EXSTDTC), is.character(ds$DSSTDTC), is.character(ho$HOSTDTC), all(table(ds$USUBJID) == 2), all(ex$USUBJID %in% dm$USUBJID), all(ho$USUBJID %in% dm$USUBJID) ) ``` ::: These are structural checks: they confirm the shape the derivations assume, not that any value is right. ::: ### Controlled terminology CDISC publishes codelists that enumerate the valid values of categorical variables. `SEX`, for instance, takes values such as `'M'`, `'F'`, and `'U'`, not `'Male'`, `'male'`, or `'1'`. The ADaM specification cites the codelist version for each controlled variable, and conformance tools reject values outside it. ### Exercises 1. Count the HF-HOME subjects by `ARM` and `ACTARM`, and compute, from `DS`, the number of disposition events of each kind by planned arm. Which counts would differ if you had grouped by `ACTARM`? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} count(dm, ARM, ACTARM) #> ARM ACTARM n #> 1 Home health Home health 1019 #> 2 Home health Usual care 197 #> 3 Usual care Home health 64 #> 4 Usual care Usual care 1152 ds |> filter(DSCAT == 'DISPOSITION EVENT') |> left_join(select(dm, USUBJID, ARM), by = 'USUBJID', relationship = 'one-to-one') |> count(ARM, DSDECOD) #> ARM DSDECOD n #> 1 Home health COMPLETED 1087 #> 2 Home health DEATH 49 #> 3 Home health LOST TO FOLLOW-UP 80 #> 4 Usual care COMPLETED 1071 #> 5 Usual care DEATH 62 #> 6 Usual care LOST TO FOLLOW-UP 83 ``` ::: Every off-diagonal cell of the first table is a subject whose received care differs from the assignment. Grouping disposition by `ACTARM` would move those subjects between arms, so every count in the second table would change. Analyses as randomized use `ARM` (in ADaM, `TRT01P`); the treatment actually received belongs to `ACTARM` (`TRT01A`), which has its own, different uses. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A colleague converts every `--DTC` variable to `Date` as soon as SDTM is read, 'to save time later'. What is lost? **Answer.** Partial dates. In a column whose first value is a complete date, `as.Date()` turns `'2024-03'` into `NA` without an error, so a collected month and year becomes missing, and the imputation rule the SAP states for partial dates can no longer be applied. Keep `--DTC` as character in SDTM and convert in ADaM, where the conversion and any imputation are part of a documented derivation (@sec-types). ::: ## ADaM: the data as analyzed {#sec-cdisc-adam} ADaM datasets take SDTM as input and produce rows and columns shaped for direct use by statistical procedures. There are three principal structures, in @tbl-adam-structures; the variables they share are collected in the ADaM variable card at the end of the chapter (@tbl-adam-card). | Structure | Rows | Examples | Key variables | |---|---|---|---| | ADSL (subject-level) | Exactly one per subject | `ADSL` | `USUBJID`, `TRT01P`, `TRT01A`, `RANDDT`, population flags | | BDS (basic data structure) | One per subject, parameter, and analysis timepoint | `ADLB`, `ADVS`, `ADTTE` | `PARAMCD`, `AVAL`, `AVISIT`, `ABLFL`, `BASE`, `CHG`, `CNSR` | | OCCDS (occurrence data structure) | One per occurrence | `ADAE`, `ADCM` | `AEDECOD`, `ASTDT`, `TRTEMFL` | : The three ADaM structures. Every other dataset joins back to `ADSL` by `USUBJID`. {#tbl-adam-structures} ### The censoring convention In an `ADTTE` dataset, `AVAL` is the time and `CNSR` is the censoring indicator. HF-HOME will use `1` for a subject followed to day 30 without an event and `2` for a subject lost to follow-up. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **`Surv(AVAL, CNSR)` runs and estimates the wrong curve.** CDISC codes the event as `CNSR = 0` and censoring as a positive integer, usually `1`, though a sponsor may use `2`, `3`, and so on for different censoring reasons. `survival::Surv()` expects the opposite: its second argument is `1` (or `TRUE`) for an event. Passed unconverted, every censored subject is treated as an event and every event as censored, so the fitted curve describes censoring, and the arm with longer follow-up looks worse. The arithmetic shortcut `Surv(AVAL, 1 - CNSR)` is right only while every censored row has `CNSR = 1`: a `CNSR = 2` becomes `-1`, which `Surv()` turns into `NA` with only a warning, and those subjects silently leave the analysis. Convert once, at the boundary, with `Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0)`, which is true for the event whatever the censoring codes are. ::: ### Analysis sets and the estimand The SAP pre-specifies which [**analysis set**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-analysis-set) each analysis uses, and ADSL implements the choice as flags. The intention-to-treat (ITT) set, or full analysis set (FAS), includes every randomized subject, analyzed as randomized (`ITTFL`, `FASFL`). A modified ITT set excludes a few randomized subjects by a rule the protocol states in advance (for example, no post-baseline assessment); its definition varies by sponsor and must be read, not assumed. The safety set includes every subject who received at least one dose, analyzed as treated (`SAFFL`). A per-protocol set excludes subjects with important protocol deviations (`PPROTFL`). An analysis set is not the estimand's population. ICH E9(R1) [@ich2019e9r1] defines the population at the level of the scientific question, and the analysis set is chosen so that the analysis estimates that estimand. For HF-HOME the SAP's estimand uses a treatment-policy strategy for nonadherence (@sec-analysis-plan-estimands): analyze every randomized subject as randomized, from randomization. Filtering on the wrong flag analyzes a different group of patients than the SAP promised, and may no longer target the stated estimand. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** The HF-HOME SAP's primary analysis is 'all randomized patients, as randomized'. Which `ADSL` variables implement that, and what changes if a programmer groups by `TRT01A` instead? **Answer.** Filter on `ITTFL == 'Y'` and group by `TRT01P`, the planned (randomized) arm. Grouping by `TRT01A` moves every nonadherent subject into the arm of the care they received, so the groups are no longer the randomized groups and the comparison is no longer protected by randomization; the treatment-policy estimand is not what it estimates. The code runs either way, which is why the specification names the variable. ::: ## Worked example: ADSL and ADTTE for HF-HOME {#sec-cdisc-worked} The derivation below builds `ADSL` and an `ADTTE` for time to readmission or death within 30 days of randomization, then analyzes it on the ITT set. The SAP's primary analysis is the 30-day risk difference (@sec-analysis-plan-worked); the time-to-event analysis here is supportive, describing when the same composite events occurred. ### Derive ADSL `ADSL` has exactly one row per subject and carries everything a downstream analysis stratifies or filters on. Each date comes from its proper source: `RANDDT` from the `RANDOMIZED` milestone in `DS`; `TRTSDT` and `TRTEDT` from the first start and last end of exposure in `EX`, never from the disposition date. Usual-care subjects who received no home-health visit have no `EX` rows, so their treatment dates are missing, which is correct. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} randomized <- ds |> filter(DSDECOD == 'RANDOMIZED') |> transmute(USUBJID, RANDDT = as.Date(DSSTDTC)) exposure <- ex |> group_by(USUBJID) |> summarize(TRTSDT = min(as.Date(EXSTDTC)), TRTEDT = max(as.Date(EXENDTC)), .groups = 'drop') arms <- c('Usual care', 'Home health') adsl <- dm |> left_join(randomized, by = 'USUBJID', relationship = 'one-to-one', unmatched = 'error') |> left_join(exposure, by = 'USUBJID', relationship = 'one-to-one') |> mutate( TRT01P = factor(ARM, levels = arms), TRT01A = factor(ACTARM, levels = arms), AGEGR1 = if_else(AGE < 65, '<65', '>=65'), ITTFL = if_else(!is.na(RANDDT), 'Y', 'N'), PPROTFL = if_else(TRT01A == TRT01P, 'Y', 'N') ) |> select(STUDYID, USUBJID, SUBJID, SITEID, AGE, AGEGR1, SEX, RACE, TRT01P, TRT01A, RANDDT, TRTSDT, TRTEDT, ITTFL, PPROTFL) stopifnot(nrow(adsl) == nrow(dm), !anyDuplicated(adsl$USUBJID)) count(adsl, TRT01P, PPROTFL) #> TRT01P PPROTFL n #> 1 Usual care N 64 #> 2 Usual care Y 1152 #> 3 Home health N 197 #> 4 Home health Y 1019 ``` ::: The per-protocol flag is included to show what it does, not to be used: restricting HF-HOME to subjects who received their assigned care compares two subsets selected after randomization, and @sec-analysis-plan-estimands explains why that targets none of the estimands the SAP could state. ### Derive ADTTE `ADTTE` is a BDS dataset: one row per subject per time-to-event parameter. The clock starts at `RANDDT`, because the estimand is defined from randomization, and the home-health visit happens after it or not at all. The event is the first of a readmission (from `HO`) or a death (from `DS`) within 30 days. A subject without an event is censored at day 30 (`CNSR = 1`), or, if lost to follow-up, at the last contact (`CNSR = 2`). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} disposition <- ds |> filter(DSCAT == 'DISPOSITION EVENT') |> transmute(USUBJID, DSDECOD, DISPDT = as.Date(DSSTDTC)) first_readmit <- ho |> group_by(USUBJID) |> summarize(READMDT = min(as.Date(HOSTDTC)), .groups = 'drop') deaths <- disposition |> filter(DSDECOD == 'DEATH') |> transmute(USUBJID, DTHDT = DISPDT) adtte <- adsl |> select(STUDYID, USUBJID, TRT01P, TRT01A, ITTFL, RANDDT) |> left_join(disposition, by = 'USUBJID', relationship = 'one-to-one', unmatched = 'error') |> left_join(first_readmit, by = 'USUBJID', relationship = 'one-to-one') |> left_join(deaths, by = 'USUBJID', relationship = 'one-to-one') |> mutate( PARAMCD = 'RDTH30', PARAM = 'Time to readmission or death within 30 days (days)', STARTDT = RANDDT, EVNTDT = pmin(READMDT, DTHDT, na.rm = TRUE), CNSR = case_when( !is.na(EVNTDT) & EVNTDT <= STARTDT + 30 ~ 0L, DSDECOD == 'LOST TO FOLLOW-UP' ~ 2L, .default = 1L), ADT = case_when( CNSR == 0L ~ EVNTDT, CNSR == 2L ~ pmin(DISPDT, STARTDT + 30), .default = STARTDT + 30), AVAL = as.numeric(ADT - STARTDT), EVNTDESC = case_when( CNSR == 0L & !is.na(READMDT) & EVNTDT == READMDT ~ 'READMISSION', CNSR == 0L ~ 'DEATH', CNSR == 2L ~ 'LOST TO FOLLOW-UP', .default = 'NO EVENT BY DAY 30') ) |> select(STUDYID, USUBJID, TRT01P, TRT01A, ITTFL, PARAMCD, PARAM, STARTDT, ADT, AVAL, CNSR, EVNTDESC) stopifnot(nrow(adtte) == nrow(adsl), all(adtte$AVAL >= 0 & adtte$AVAL <= 30)) count(adtte, CNSR, EVNTDESC) #> CNSR EVNTDESC n #> 1 0 DEATH 79 #> 2 0 READMISSION 429 #> 3 1 NO EVENT BY DAY 30 1761 #> 4 2 LOST TO FOLLOW-UP 163 ``` ::: `AVAL` here is `ADT - STARTDT`; many sponsors add one day so that an event on the start date has `AVAL = 1`. Either is defensible, and the specification states which.[^aval] [^aval]: The SAP and the ADaM specification should agree on this and on the censoring date for subjects lost to follow-up (last contact, here; some plans use the last date of known status). Neither choice changes the estimand; both change `AVAL`. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Re-derive the event count and the event days from the raw outcome file, which never passed through SDTM, and compare. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} raw_events <- read_hf('outcomes.csv') |> filter(event_30d == 1) |> transmute(USUBJID = paste('HFHOME', patient_id, sep = '-'), days = days_to_event) adtte_events <- adtte |> filter(CNSR == 0) |> select(USUBJID, days = AVAL) stopifnot( nrow(raw_events) == nrow(adtte_events), isTRUE(all.equal(arrange(raw_events, USUBJID), arrange(adtte_events, USUBJID), check.attributes = FALSE)) ) nrow(adtte_events) #> [1] 508 ``` ::: Two derivations from different sources that agree subject by subject are evidence that the censoring logic is right; a count that agrees and days that do not would point at the date logic. ::: ### Analyze from ADTTE The analysis filters on the ITT flag and converts the censoring code once, at the boundary, with `CNSR == 0`. HF-HOME's `ADTTE` contains `CNSR = 2`, so this is not a matter of style: `1 - CNSR` would drop the subjects lost to follow-up. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} analysis <- adtte |> filter(ITTFL == 'Y', PARAMCD == 'RDTH30') fit <- survfit(Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = analysis) summary(fit, times = 30) #> Call: survfit(formula = Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = analysis) #> #> TRT01P=Usual care #> time n.risk n.event survival std.err lower 95% CI #> 30.0000 871.0000 268.0000 0.7650 0.0126 0.7408 #> upper 95% CI #> 0.7901 #> #> TRT01P=Home health #> time n.risk n.event survival std.err lower 95% CI #> 30.0000 912.0000 240.0000 0.7951 0.0118 0.7723 #> upper 95% CI #> 0.8186 cox <- coxph(Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0) ~ TRT01P, data = analysis) hr <- summary(cox)$conf.int hr #> exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95 #> TRT01PHome health 0.8517262 1.174086 0.7155703 1.013789 stopifnot(cox$n == nrow(analysis)) ``` ::: The hazard ratio for home health against usual care is 0.85 (95% confidence interval 0.72 to 1.01). The interval includes 1, so this supportive analysis, like the primary one, is inconclusive: it neither shows that home health reduces early readmission or death nor rules out a reduction of the size the trial was designed to detect. The `stopifnot()` confirms that no subject was dropped on the way into the model. @fig-cdisc-km shows the cumulative incidence by arm, with the risk table that regulatory reviewers expect beneath the curve. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(survminer) ggsurvplot(fit, data = analysis, fun = 'event', conf.int = TRUE, risk.table = TRUE, break.time.by = 10, xlab = 'Days from randomization', ylab = 'Cumulative incidence', legend.title = 'Arm', legend.labs = arms, ggtheme = theme_minimal()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Cumulative incidence of readmission or death within 30 days of randomization, by randomized arm, from the HF-HOME ADTTE (ITT set). Shaded bands are pointwise 95% confidence intervals; the table beneath gives the number still at risk.](19-cdisc_files/figure-html/fig-cdisc-km-1.png){#fig-cdisc-km fig-align='center' fig-alt='Two rising step curves of cumulative incidence over 30 days, one per randomized arm, with overlapping shaded confidence bands; the usual-care curve lies slightly above the home-health curve. A risk table beneath the axis lists the number of subjects still at risk in each arm at days 0, 10, 20, and 30.' fig-scap='Cumulative incidence from the HF-HOME ADTTE' width=100%} ::: ::: The row granularity changed at every step, and tracking it is the skill: `dm` has one row per subject, `ex` one per home-health visit, `ds` two per subject, `ho` one per readmission; `adsl` returns to one per subject and `adtte` has one per subject per parameter. The declared `relationship =` on every join and the `stopifnot()` after each derivation are the minimum. ### Exercises 2. Stack a second parameter into `ADTTE`: time to death within 30 days (`PARAMCD = 'DTH30'`), censored at day 30 or at last contact as before. Verify that the stacked dataset has two rows per subject and that its number of `DTH30` events equals the number of `DEATH` records in `DS`. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} adtte_dth <- adsl |> select(STUDYID, USUBJID, TRT01P, TRT01A, ITTFL, RANDDT) |> left_join(disposition, by = 'USUBJID', relationship = 'one-to-one', unmatched = 'error') |> left_join(deaths, by = 'USUBJID', relationship = 'one-to-one') |> mutate( PARAMCD = 'DTH30', PARAM = 'Time to death within 30 days (days)', STARTDT = RANDDT, CNSR = case_when( !is.na(DTHDT) ~ 0L, DSDECOD == 'LOST TO FOLLOW-UP' ~ 2L, .default = 1L), ADT = case_when( CNSR == 0L ~ DTHDT, CNSR == 2L ~ pmin(DISPDT, STARTDT + 30), .default = STARTDT + 30), AVAL = as.numeric(ADT - STARTDT), EVNTDESC = case_when( CNSR == 0L ~ 'DEATH', CNSR == 2L ~ 'LOST TO FOLLOW-UP', .default = 'NO EVENT BY DAY 30') ) |> select(all_of(names(adtte))) adtte2 <- bind_rows(adtte, adtte_dth) stopifnot( nrow(adtte2) == 2 * nrow(adsl), all(count(adtte2, USUBJID)$n == 2), sum(adtte2$PARAMCD == 'DTH30' & adtte2$CNSR == 0) == sum(ds$DSDECOD == 'DEATH') ) count(adtte2, PARAMCD, CNSR) #> PARAMCD CNSR n #> 1 DTH30 0 111 #> 2 DTH30 1 2158 #> 3 DTH30 2 163 #> 4 RDTH30 0 508 #> 5 RDTH30 1 1761 #> 6 RDTH30 2 163 ``` ::: BDS datasets grow downward: a second endpoint is more rows with a different `PARAMCD`, never a second `AVAL` column. `select(all_of(names(adtte)))` keeps the two blocks stackable; `bind_rows()` of frames with different columns succeeds and fills the gaps with `NA`, which is how a BDS dataset quietly acquires columns that apply to one parameter only. Deaths are a subset of the composite events, so the `DTH30` event count must be smaller than the `RDTH30` count; deaths after a readmission are events here and not there. ::: 3. Build a minimal BDS `ADLB` for NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide) from `labs.csv` and `visits.csv`: one row per subject per analysis visit (`AVISIT` of `'BASELINE'` for discharge and `'DAY 30'` for the day-30 clinic), with `AVAL`, `ABLFL`, `BASE`, and `CHG`. Restrict it to randomized subjects, and assert one row per subject and visit. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} visit_map <- read_hf('visits.csv') |> filter(visit_type %in% c('discharge', 'clinic_day30')) |> select(visit_id, visit_type) adlb <- read_hf('labs.csv') |> filter(test_code == 'NTPROBNP') |> distinct(patient_id, visit_id, test_code, value) |> inner_join(visit_map, by = 'visit_id', relationship = 'one-to-one') |> transmute(USUBJID = paste('HFHOME', patient_id, sep = '-'), PARAMCD = 'NTPROBNP', AVISIT = if_else(visit_type == 'discharge', 'BASELINE', 'DAY 30'), AVAL = value) |> semi_join(adsl, by = 'USUBJID') |> group_by(USUBJID) |> mutate(ABLFL = if_else(AVISIT == 'BASELINE', 'Y', NA_character_), BASE = AVAL[AVISIT == 'BASELINE'][1], CHG = if_else(AVISIT == 'BASELINE', NA_real_, AVAL - BASE)) |> ungroup() stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(adlb[c('USUBJID', 'AVISIT')]), all(adlb$USUBJID %in% adsl$USUBJID)) count(adlb, AVISIT) #> # A tibble: 2 × 2 #> AVISIT n #> #> 1 BASELINE 2432 #> 2 DAY 30 1648 ``` ::: Two planted defects meet this derivation. The exact duplicate of one discharge NT-proBNP row is removed by `distinct()` on all columns, which is safe only because the rows are identical; the assertion after it would catch a conflicting pair. The orphan patient `2433` has labs but no visit record, so the inner join to `visits` already drops it; the `semi_join()` to `ADSL` states the rule that guarantees it, because ADaM contains randomized subjects only. `ABLFL` is `'Y'` or missing, never `'N'`, as for every ADaM flag of this kind. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Why does the HF-HOME `ADTTE` start the clock at `RANDDT` rather than `TRTSDT`? **Answer.** Because the estimand is defined for every randomized subject from randomization, and `TRTSDT` (the first home-health visit) is missing for most usual-care subjects and comes after randomization for the rest. Starting at `TRTSDT` would drop or shift exactly the subjects whose care differed from assignment, and the comparison would no longer be between randomized groups. ::: ## Industry practice: tables, validation, double programming {#sec-cdisc-industry} ### The pharmaverse Until the late 2010s, almost all ADaM work in industry was done in SAS (@sec-sas). Since about 2022, the year `admiral` [@mancini2026admiral] first reached CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network), a cross-company collaboration called the [**pharmaverse**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-pharmaverse) has produced R packages for each step of the pipeline: `admiral` for ADaM derivations, `metacore` and `metatools` to read and apply specifications, and `xportr` to write the SAS transport (XPT) files the FDA requires. At a sponsor that has adopted R, expect these in production. ### Tables, listings, and figures Every table in a CSR is built from ADaM, and several R packages build them. `gtsummary` [@sjoberg2021gtsummary] is the general one; the demographics table below is computed from `ADSL`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(gtsummary) adsl |> filter(ITTFL == 'Y') |> select(TRT01P, AGE, AGEGR1, SEX) |> tbl_summary(by = TRT01P, label = list(AGE ~ 'Age, years', AGEGR1 ~ 'Age group', SEX ~ 'Sex')) |> add_overall() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Two families are built for regulatory output. `rtables`, with the analysis functions of `tern`, describes a table as a layout that is then applied to the data; `Tplyr` builds a table from layers of counts and descriptive statistics. Neither is installed in this book's environment, so the code is display-only and unverified here: ```r library(rtables) library(tern) basic_table() |> split_cols_by('TRT01P') |> add_overall_col('All') |> analyze_vars(c('AGE', 'SEX')) |> build_table(adsl) library(Tplyr) tplyr_table(adsl, TRT01P) |> add_layer(group_desc(AGE)) |> add_layer(group_count(SEX)) |> build() ``` ### R in submissions and validated packages R is accepted in submissions. The R Consortium's R Submissions Working Group has run pilot submissions to FDA built in R. Pilot 1, four TLFs, received FDA's final review response in March 2022; Pilot 2, a Shiny application, received its response in September 2023; Pilot 3, ADaM datasets and TLFs built in R, received its final response letter in August 2024; and Pilot 4, the Shiny application delivered through WebAssembly and through a container, received FDA's review letter in May 2026.[^pilots] These are test submissions, not drug approvals. What a sponsor must show is that the software it relies on is fit for purpose. The R Validation Hub, another R Consortium working group, publishes a risk-based approach to that question, and its `riskmetric` package scores a package on documentation, testing, maintenance, and use (display-only; not installed here): ```r library(riskmetric) pkg_ref('survival') |> pkg_assess() |> pkg_score() ``` [^pilots]: As of 2026-10. Dates are from the working group's pilot pages (`rconsortium.github.io/submissions-wg`), the pilot repositories on GitHub (`github.com/RConsortium`), and R Consortium announcements of August 2024 (Pilot 3) and May 2026 (Pilot 4). Pilot 5, which replaces XPT with Dataset-JSON, was resubmitted in January 2026; check its repository for the current status before citing it. ### Double programming The standard validation of an ADaM dataset or a table in industry is [**double programming**](F-glossary.qmd#gloss-double-programming): a second programmer derives the same output independently from the specification, without reading the first programmer's code, and the two outputs are compared value by value. Any difference is investigated until both agree or the specification is clarified. The `diffdf` package is the usual comparison tool in R (display-only; not installed here): ```r diffdf::diffdf(base = adtte, compare = adtte_qc, keys = 'USUBJID') ``` The chunk below is the same idea with tools already loaded: an independent derivation of the whole `ADTTE`, from the raw CSV files rather than from SDTM, compared row by row. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} last_contact <- read_hf('visits.csv') |> group_by(patient_id) |> summarize(last_day = max(visit_day), .groups = 'drop') adtte_qc <- read_hf('outcomes.csv') |> left_join(last_contact, by = 'patient_id', relationship = 'one-to-one') |> transmute( USUBJID = paste('HFHOME', patient_id, sep = '-'), AVAL = case_when(event_30d == 1 ~ days_to_event, !ascertained ~ pmin(last_day, 30), .default = 30), CNSR = case_when(event_30d == 1 ~ 0L, !ascertained ~ 2L, .default = 1L) ) |> arrange(USUBJID) primary <- adtte |> select(USUBJID, AVAL, CNSR) |> arrange(USUBJID) mismatches <- primary |> inner_join(adtte_qc, by = 'USUBJID', suffix = c('', '_qc'), relationship = 'one-to-one', unmatched = 'error') |> filter(AVAL != AVAL_qc | CNSR != CNSR_qc) stopifnot(nrow(mismatches) == 0) nrow(mismatches) #> [1] 0 ``` ::: The QC derivation shares no code and no intermediate dataset with the primary one: it uses `visits.csv` for the last contact where the primary used the `DS` date, and the outcome flags where the primary used `HO` and `DS`. Agreement on all 2432 subjects is evidence about the derivation; a second run of the same code would be evidence about nothing. ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} An independent re-derivation by a model is the AI analogue of double programming, and it has the same rule: the second derivation must not see the first. > **Context.** I am validating an ADaM `ADTTE` dataset. The > specification is below: [the `ADTTE` rows of the ADaM > specification, with each variable's source and derivation]. > The source files are described by these variable lists and > types: [column names and types of `outcomes.csv` and > `visits.csv`, and three synthetic rows of each]. > > **Constraints.** Write an R function that derives `USUBJID`, > `AVAL`, and `CNSR` from the two source files using `dplyr` > only. Use `CNSR = 0` for the event and the positive codes in > the specification for censoring. Declare `relationship =` on > every join. Do not ask for, and do not use, any existing > derivation code. > > **Criteria.** List every assumption you make where the > specification is silent (the censoring date for a subject lost > to follow-up, the treatment of a death after a readmission). > I will compare your output to the primary dataset subject by > subject. *Failure mode.* A model shown the primary code reproduces its errors, which defeats the comparison; a model not shown the specification invents a censoring rule, often `CNSR = 1` for every censored subject. *Check.* Run its function on the real files inside your environment and compare with the `mismatches` join above, which must return no rows; investigate every assumption it listed against the SAP. Real SDTM and ADaM are individual patient data and the sponsor's confidential information: send the specification and synthetic rows, never the datasets (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A programmer validates an `ADTTE` by re-running the primary program on a second machine and comparing outputs. They agree exactly. What has been shown? **Answer.** That the program is deterministic, not that it is correct. Double programming is valuable because the second derivation is independent: different code, written from the specification by someone who has not seen the first, so that a shared misreading is unlikely. A misread censoring rule survives any number of re-runs of the same code. ::: ## Rules of thumb 1. **Habit 2: raw data are evidence; derived data are a build product.** SDTM is never edited; every analytic decision becomes an ADaM variable with a documented derivation. 2. **Habit 6: count before and after every join.** One row per subject in `ADSL`, one per subject per parameter in `ADTTE`; declare the relationship and assert the counts at every step. 3. **Habit 9: test the statistics, not the shape.** A dataset with the right columns can carry the wrong censoring; an independent derivation compared value by value is the test. ## Cumulative practice 4. *Cumulative (uses @sec-analysis-plan).* Write the ADaM specification for the HF-HOME `ADTTE` as a table with one row per variable (name, label, type, source, derivation), with the derivations stated so that a second programmer could implement them without this chapter's code. Then assert in R that every variable in `adtte` appears in your specification and no specification row is missing from `adtte`. 5. *On your own work (no key).* Install `admiral` and `pharmaverseadam`, and compare `pharmaverseadam::adsl` with the `ADSL` built here. List the variables that the simplified version lacks, and for each, say which analysis would need it. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution to exercise 4'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} adtte_spec <- tribble( ~variable, ~label, ~source, 'STUDYID', 'Study identifier', 'ADSL.STUDYID', 'USUBJID', 'Unique subject identifier', 'ADSL.USUBJID', 'TRT01P', 'Planned treatment', 'ADSL.TRT01P', 'TRT01A', 'Actual treatment', 'ADSL.TRT01A', 'ITTFL', 'ITT population flag', 'ADSL.ITTFL', 'PARAMCD', 'Parameter code', 'Assigned', 'PARAM', 'Parameter', 'Assigned', 'STARTDT', 'Time-to-event origin date', 'ADSL.RANDDT', 'ADT', 'Analysis date', 'HO.HOSTDTC, DS.DSSTDTC', 'AVAL', 'Analysis value (days)', 'ADT - STARTDT', 'CNSR', 'Censor (0 = event)', 'HO, DS', 'EVNTDESC', 'Event or censoring description', 'HO, DS' ) stopifnot(setequal(adtte_spec$variable, names(adtte))) adtte_spec #> # A tibble: 12 × 3 #> variable label source #> #> 1 STUDYID Study identifier ADSL.STUDYID #> 2 USUBJID Unique subject identifier ADSL.USUBJID #> 3 TRT01P Planned treatment ADSL.TRT01P #> 4 TRT01A Actual treatment ADSL.TRT01A #> 5 ITTFL ITT population flag ADSL.ITTFL #> 6 PARAMCD Parameter code Assigned #> 7 PARAM Parameter Assigned #> 8 STARTDT Time-to-event origin date ADSL.RANDDT #> 9 ADT Analysis date HO.HOSTDTC, DS.DSSTDTC #> 10 AVAL Analysis value (days) ADT - STARTDT #> 11 CNSR Censor (0 = event) HO, DS #> 12 EVNTDESC Event or censoring description HO, DS ``` ::: A full specification adds a type and a derivation column; the derivation for `CNSR`, for instance, reads '0 if the first of `HO.HOSTDTC` (readmission) or `DS.DSSTDTC` where `DS.DSDECOD = 'DEATH'` falls within 30 days of `STARTDT`; 2 if `DS.DSDECOD = 'LOST TO FOLLOW-UP'`; otherwise 1'. The `setequal()` check is a structural check: it confirms that the specification and the dataset name the same variables, not that the derivations agree. The double-programming comparison in @sec-cdisc-industry is the check on the values. ::: ## Cheat sheet | Variable | Dataset | Meaning | Trap | |---|---|---|---| | `USUBJID` | All | Unique subject identifier, study-wide | Join on it, never on `SUBJID` alone | | `TRT01P`, `TRT01A` | ADSL | Planned and actual treatment, period 1 | As-randomized analyses use `TRT01P` | | `RANDDT` | ADSL | Randomization date, from `DS` | The origin for ITT time-to-event | | `TRTSDT`, `TRTEDT` | ADSL | First and last exposure, from `EX` | Not from the disposition date | | `ITTFL`, `FASFL` | ADSL | Randomized, analyzed as randomized | The set is not the estimand's population | | `SAFFL` | ADSL | Received any treatment, analyzed as treated | Not an efficacy set | | `PPROTFL` | ADSL | No important protocol deviations | Selected after randomization | | `PARAMCD`, `PARAM` | BDS | Parameter code (8 characters at most) and name | New endpoint, new rows | | `AVAL`, `AVALC` | BDS | Analysis value, numeric and character | Units belong in `PARAM` | | `AVISIT`, `AVISITN` | BDS | Analysis visit, character and numeric | Not the collected `VISIT` | | `ABLFL`, `BASE`, `CHG` | BDS | Baseline flag, baseline value, change | Flags are `'Y'` or missing, never `'N'` | | `STARTDT`, `ADT` | ADTTE | Origin and event or censoring date | `AVAL` convention: with or without `+ 1` | | `CNSR` | ADTTE | 0 = event; positive = censored, by reason | `Surv(AVAL, CNSR == 0)` | | `EVNTDESC` | ADTTE | Event or censoring description | Must agree with `CNSR` | | `ANL01FL` | BDS | Record used in an analysis | Filter on it when the SAP says so | | `ASTDT`, `TRTEMFL` | OCCDS | Analysis start date; treatment-emergent flag | Window usually closes at `TRTEDT` plus a lag; partial dates need a rule | : The ADaM variable card. {#tbl-adam-card} ## Further reading - CDISC Foundational Standards at `cdisc.org/standards/foundational`, the authoritative reference for SDTM and ADaM. - [@mancini2026admiral], the `admiral` package and its vignettes, which derive every common ADaM dataset in R. - [@fda2024conformance], the FDA Study Data Technical Conformance Guide, which states what a submission must contain. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-19} 1. SDTM (Study Data Tabulation Model) holds the submitted record of the collected clinical data, organized into domains such as `DM`, `AE`, `LB`, and `EX`. ADaM (Analysis Data Model) holds analysis-ready datasets derived from SDTM. In industry, statistical programmers typically build ADaM against specifications written or reviewed by the biostatistician, who also writes the SAP; SDTM is built by data management or clinical programmers. 2. A censored observation. `CNSR = 0` is the event, and other positive integers may code other censoring reasons; pass `CNSR == 0` to `survival::Surv()` as the event. 3. `ADSL` is the subject-level anchor dataset, with exactly one row per subject: treatment assignment, demographics, baseline covariates, key dates, and population flags. Every other ADaM dataset (`ADLB`, `ADTTE`, `ADAE`) joins back to `ADSL` by `USUBJID` and takes treatment and population flags from it.
